# 14-code-four — sources

Back-test entry `14-code-four.yaml`: Code Four, police reports drafted from body-cam footage (YC Spring 2025, X25).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's choice"

2025-05-23 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one exists;

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

screens.why5: The belief and the test read back my pick word for word, 'nothing is reworded here' holds, and the 1-in-3 bar is a fair reading of 'most'.

screens.why1: After how it fits the way officers work today, asking what it does better than writing the report by hand is the obvious next step for the solution.
screens.why2: "What does it do better than the way they do it today" with a 25-word cap is plain to me as a founder who pitches desk time to chiefs every day.
screens.why3: I know exactly what we beat: the hour at the desk per report and the facts that get missed when an officer is down 10 reports, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: A free-text box with "Leave this out of the study" as the escape fits a benefit question, and the escape is a real choice if I didn't want to test advantage.
screens.why5: Keel kept "minutes, not an hour" but dropped my second benefit, "nothing on the footage left out", and "their last call would have gone better" slides from the report to the call itself, when the call was fine and the paperwork was the pain.
screens.instead: For most, the report from their last call would have been better with it: done in minutes, not an hour, and nothing on the footage left out.

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, Keel shows the benefits it drew from that and asks me to check them, so it is obvious why this comes here.
screens.why2: Both rows are in a cop's own words: a report in minutes, not an hour, and nothing on the footage missed are what my officers and chiefs say to me.
screens.why3: Every patrol officer knows how long their last report took and whether they had to scrub back through the footage, so they can answer from their own shift.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and plain, but my headline benefit is missing: getting the officer off the desk and back on patrol instead of clocking out late.
screens.why5: The rows keep my claims (desk time cut, every frame read), but the test says their last *call* would have gone better, when what we improve is the report after the call, not the call itself.
screens.instead: Rows: The report done in minutes, not an hour / Nothing on the footage left out / Off the desk and back on patrol sooner. Test: For most, the report from their last call would have been done faster with it.

screens.why1: Right after compatibility and relative advantage, asking what it costs an officer to take up the tool is the obvious next piece of the solution step.
screens.why2: "To start using it" made me think first of our 48-hour setup, when what I mean is the work an officer does on every report; I had to lean on the hint to see that per-draft steps count.
screens.why3: I know exactly what an officer has to do with our draft: review it, fix it, and strip the check words before it will submit.
screens.why4: There's only a free-text box and the escape chip, and "Leave this out of the study" is a fair way out for a founder who doesn't want to test friction.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my tested item word for word, reading and correcting every draft before signing, and leaves my second line, the check words, as the untested one, which is what I meant.
screens.instead: What will an officer have to do on every report that they don't do today? (Any setup, extra steps or learning. Up to 25 words.)

screens.why1: After telling Keel what officers must do to start, checking its list of those steps is the obvious next screen, and it is the last of the four solution parts.
screens.why2: Draft, signing, check words and body-cam footage are my own words and my trade's, so I read every row at first sight.
screens.why3: These are the exact steps my officers take with Code Four: review the draft, strip the planted check words, and get the footage in.
screens.why4: The first two rows are right, but uploading footage is something officers already do when they dock the camera, and it repeats the upload condition I set under fit, so it is not a new step our product asks of them.
screens.why5: The tested belief, that most would read and correct every draft before signing, is what I typed: patrol reviews reports instead of writing them from scratch.
screens.instead: Rows: Read and correct every draft before signing; Find and delete the check words in each draft; Pick which call's footage to draft from. Test the first.

screens.why1: After I've said what officers must do to start using Code Four, the next step is to pick the effort most likely to stop them; that is the step the study tests, so it belongs here.
screens.why2: Draft, signing and check words are my own words and plain to me and to a patrol officer; the title and intro read at once.
screens.why3: Whether officers will actually read and fix every draft before they sign is the thing I live with in every pilot, so I can answer it from what I know.
screens.why4: Reading and correcting, and deleting check words, are real efforts that are distinct from each other, but uploading the footage is something officers already do when they dock the camera, and it repeats the upload condition I tested under Compatibility, so it overlaps.
screens.why5: The pick and the belief keep my words exactly ('Read and correct every draft before signing'), and none of my product's name or roles leaks into the test.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? — Read and correct every draft before signing / Find and delete the check words in each draft / Get the drafts typed into our records system

screens.why1: A free, no-strings pilot is how I sign departments, so asking whether to offer one just before the study goes out is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is my everyday word, and the hint shows exactly the line respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want a pilot list is my own call, and I know I do: I fly out and set agencies up within 48 hours.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, and the two options are distinct and in plain words.
screens.why5: My 'Yes' is kept, and the respondent's line, 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.', leaks nothing of Code Four or the chief's role.

screens.why1: Choosing who interviews the officers belongs in the last step before the study goes out, right after deciding on the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint says the AI asks on video and then talks only about recording a voice, so I have to read it twice to tell whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both.
screens.why3: I know my officers and how they react to a stranger asking about their reports, so I can pick who they'd listen to.
screens.why4: Two names with five-second samples are distinct and the preselect works, but both sound like the same kind of interviewer, and there's no option a patrol audience might take to more readily, such as a different-sounding voice.
screens.why5: It keeps 'patrol officers' as I typed it, and nothing of Code Four leaks into who asks.
screens.instead: Who should ask patrol officers your questions on video? (Daphne ▶ hear · Saskia ▶ hear) — hint: you pick the face and voice once for this project, 400 credits either way; officers get the link by text and can read and tap instead of talking.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it makes sense to choose how patrol officers will answer before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Talking, typing or tapping is plain to me, and the line about loud places reads straight to an officer on a highway shoulder or in a cruiser; the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' looks like a name label running into its description, not a word I would trip on.
screens.why3: I know how my officers live, phone in hand between calls or at the end of a shift, so I can say whether they would rather talk to a video or read and tap.
screens.why4: AI voice, read-and-tap, or let them pick covers every real choice, the three are distinct, and the readiness note on each tells me what I would wait for.
screens.why5: It speaks of patrol officers as I typed them and nothing of Code Four's product leaks into the choice.

screens.why1: Choosing who gets a link is the obvious last step after picking how patrol officers answer, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The three choices are plain to me as a founder using Keel; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen, and the rest is everyday words.
screens.why3: I reach officers mostly through chiefs at design-partner agencies, so I would have to guess how many officers I know by name, as opposed to a chief forwarding the link at roll call.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and one open link are distinct and cover how I would reach officers; the department-forwarded route fits under the open link, though 'signs in with Google' may snag officers on department accounts.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed or leaked; the screen asks only how the links go out.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside the deciding number, 4 answered, and every card adds '5 needed to call it', so I know nothing is decided and why.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart; the tally '3 too few · 7 people answered' needs a second look because the cards say only 4 answered, and the screen never says what happened to the other 3.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the exact belief lines I checked, though the solution statement above them is garbled and repeats itself.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, such as getting one more officer's answer per card or explaining why 3 of 7 were not counted.
screens.why_b5: No belief is claimed as held or failed; the low n is stated outright on every card.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of your 7 answered each solution question and 5 are needed; the other 3 were not asked these questions (say why). Get at least one more patrol officer to answer and all three beliefs can be read.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its deciding number, 4 counted of the 5 needed, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: It is clear that 4 counted officers all said yes, but 'against your bar · 3 of 4 (no more than 1 in 3 say no)' reads as if 3 of 4 were against me, so I had to look twice to see the bar was met with 0 saying no.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'For most patrol officers, the footage was uploaded before the shift ended' are exactly what I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not tell me that one more counted officer would settle it, or that all four so far uploaded in time.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Luis's guess is shown as not counted, and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', so nothing is claimed beyond four officers.
screens.instead: All 4 counted officers had their footage up before the shift ended, none said no; one more counted answer settles it, so get one more officer, ideally one whose camera only uploads at the dock.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted of 5 needed, and the count line explains the gap: Luis's answer was a guess.
screens.why_b2: I can see 3 'a lot better' and 1 'no difference' out of 4, but 'your bar · 3 of 4' next to a rule of 'no more than 1 in 3 against' took a second look, and so did the ghost fifth cell in the strip.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and 'the report done in minutes, not an hour' are the words I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that 3 of 4 already leans my way or that one more counted officer would decide it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', the hypothetical framing is flagged, and nothing is claimed as held.
screens.instead: 3 of 4 officers say a lot better, which is above my bar, but I need one more counted answer to call it; Luis's answer was a guess, so get one more officer to answer.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted against 5 needed, and the So line repeats that same pair.
screens.why_b2: The four bars and the 3-of-4 marker are plain, but the strip's ghost cell needs a second look: it could be Luis or the missing fifth answer, and a bar of 3 of 4 next to '5 needed' takes a moment to square.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Adoption friction and the belief line is word for word the one I checked: 'Most would read and correct every draft before signing.'
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that all four counted lean my way (two only if it's clearly worth it), or that one more countable answer, such as re-asking Luis plainly, would settle it.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said honestly ('a lean, not a call'), but the status line reads '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', a soft mix-up of answered and counted.
screens.instead: Four of four counted would read and correct every draft (two only if it's clearly worth it), but that's one short of a call: get one more officer's plain answer (Luis's was a guess) to settle it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no answer yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: 'Relative advantage' and 'For most, their last call would have gone better with it: the report done in minutes, not an hour.' are word for word the dimension and belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more answer, but the screen never says so, and it says nothing about what Kenji's answer means for the idea, such as aiming the minutes-not-an-hour claim at long arrest reports rather than simple ones.
screens.why_b5: The low n is stated plainly, the against count is one of one asked, and nothing is called held or strong; the trailing 'No difference / against' tags are terse but claim nothing beyond the data.
screens.why_b6: Kenji's answer adds something I did not type: simple reports already get written in the car between calls, and short staffing, not paperwork, is what makes calls stack up, so my time saving may only bite on the long reports.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 answered, so ask one more officer. The one against writes simple reports in the car and says being two cars short is the bigger pain, so test whether the hour saved is on long reports like DUI arrests.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious why they ask; the study is about departments my size, so they check that before anything else.
screens.why2: Plain to me: I know roughly how many sworn officers we have, and I answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know my own department's headcount, so I can answer this without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly for a gate, and no escape is right on a screener.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 10-to-200 segment exactly, and nothing about a product or report tool leaks to me.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is stiff for a screener; the 2026-10-31 amendment says the screener's spoken form is just the stem then 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Does the department you work for now have between 10 and 200 officers? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After the department-size check, asking whether I actually went back to body-cam footage for a report this week is the obvious next gate before asking me to tell about a call.
screens.why2: Body-cam footage and writing a report are my everyday words, and I can answer this on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I pulled up my own footage to write a report this past week; it is my shift.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate should carry no escape: 'I'd rather not say' is not supposed to exist, and 'I can't recall one particular call' does not answer a yes-or-no about the whole week.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's situation of footage still having to become a report, and nothing about a product or their terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question ending in 'Yes or no', easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you go back through your body-cam footage to write a report? Yes · No (no escape chips on this gate)

screens.why1: Right after I said I rewatched my body-cam to write a report, showing me a tool that drafts the report from that footage is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Most of it is how I'd talk about a report, but 'It has check words you must catch' made me stop: I'd guess it means planted errors I have to find before signing, and it doesn't say so, while 'a drafted narrative report' as the name for a tool reads wrong.
screens.why3: Uploading a call's footage, writing the narrative in our records format, reviewing and signing are all things I do every shift.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: Calling Code Four 'a drafted narrative report' instead of a tool that drafts one, and the bare 'check words', sound like the builder's own shorthand, and the tacked-on redaction and search pull it away from the report itself.
screens.why6: Heard once it mostly holds, but 'it has check words you must catch' and 'redacts footage in one click and searches it' crowd in at the end, so by the belief line I've lost the thread.
screens.instead: Imagine Code Four, a tool that drafts your incident report from body-cam footage. You upload a call's footage and it writes the narrative in your department's report format, with each fact linked to its clip, and a few planted mistakes you must find before you sign. The people building it believe it would let you review and sign instead of writing from scratch.

screens.why1: Asking whether my footage was up before end of shift makes sense for a tool that writes from body-cam, but the card only said 'a drafted narrative report' and never said it works from the footage, so the jump to uploads comes out of nowhere.
screens.why2: 'Had your footage uploaded' is broken English that I'd have to read twice, and it could mean 'did you upload it' or 'did it finish syncing'; I'd say 'Was your footage uploaded before you went end of watch?'
screens.why3: I know whether my camera got docked and synced to Evidence before I clocked out on my last call, so I can answer this from my own shift.
screens.why4: Yes and No fit, but 'Yes, with some steps' means nothing for a camera upload; the real middle answer is 'only after I docked it at the station' or 'part of it', and 'I can't tell' fits since sometimes you don't know if the sync finished.
screens.why5: Code Four on the card is shown on purpose and 'narrative' is our word, but 'a drafted narrative report' doesn't say what the thing is, and asking about upload before shift end has likely drifted from whatever the founder actually needs the footage to be ready for.
screens.why6: It is short, has three options and one escape, but the stem 'Had your footage uploaded before your shift ended' sounds garbled when heard once and the 'with some steps' option makes you stop and think.
screens.instead: Think of your last call. Was your body-cam footage uploaded before you wrote the report? Yes; yes, after I docked the camera; no, it was still on the camera -- or I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the footage question, it makes sense to ask whether this would have helped me on my last call.
screens.why2: To me the call is the scene itself, and nothing would have changed out there, so 'made your last call go better' makes me stop and work out that you mean the report I wrote afterwards.
screens.why3: I can say whether a drafted narrative would have saved me time on that report, but I'd be guessing at how it changes 'the call', since the card never says it works from my body-cam footage.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it without overlap, and 'I can't tell' is an honest out after a one-line card.
screens.why5: Calling Code Four 'a drafted narrative report' sounds like the report itself rather than something that drafts my narrative from the footage, and the question has moved from the report to the call.
screens.why6: It is short, asks one thing, and four short options plus the escape are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Would Code Four have made the report from your last call easier to write, or not? A lot easier; a little easier; no difference; or harder. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After asking whether it would have helped my last call, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually go through and fix every draft it wrote before I put my name on it.
screens.why2: Read and correct the draft before I sign it is exactly how I'd say it; I sign every report I turn in, so nothing here needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd go line by line through a draft before signing, since my name is on it and I'll be testifying to it in court.
screens.why4: 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' reads odd for me because reviewing a report I sign isn't optional, so the real split is whether it saves me time after the fixes, and 'probably not' and 'no' sit close together.
screens.why5: The card names the thing on purpose, and the question just states the condition of using it without slipping in any vendor or sales language I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: Heard once it's short, one question, four short options I can hold, and the single escape comes last.
screens.instead: If Code Four's draft still needed you to check and fix every line before you signed it, would you use it, or not? Yes · Yes, if fixing it was quicker than writing · Probably not · No · I can't tell
